options: The rate at which velocity changes
The speed reached at the finish
The push that starts a race
questions.explanation: Acceleration answers how quickly velocity changes per second — it is the rate of change of velocity, not a distance or a finish speed.
questions.misconception: Learners often reduce acceleration to 'going faster'; slowing down and turning are accelerations too, because velocity encompasses direction.

questions.prompt: A car speeds from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its average acceleration?
questions.misconception: Adding (20+5=25), doubling (100), or picking the final speed (20) shows the formula seat-belt error — always subtract first, then divide.

questions.prompt: A car brakes from 15 m/s to 0 m/s in 3 s. What is the sign of its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Braking reduces velocity, and a decrease shows up as a negative (final − initial). Negative acceleration is still acceleration.
questions.misconception: Some think braking is the absence of acceleration. It's acceleration pointing opposite the motion — a negative value, not no value.

questions.prompt: A train cruises at a steady 22 m/s on straight track. What is its acceleration?
options: It keeps accelerating all the time
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means velocity doesn't change, so acceleration is zero — cruising is not the same as accelerating.
questions.misconception: Motion itself is drained to stand for acceleration; movement is not acceleration, change of velocity is.

questions.prompt: On a velocity-time graph, what does the slope represent?
questions.explanation: Slope on a velocity-time graph is (velocity change) ÷ (time change), which is exactly the definition of acceleration.
questions.misconception: The slope of distance-time is speed; people carry that habit over and mislabel this graph's slope as speed.
